stem: A retail chief information officer opens the first meeting with an architect by saying: "We need a Claude chatbot for returns. How fast can you build it?" Nobody has yet described the current returns process, its volumes, or what a wrong answer costs. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Propose a retrieval-augmented chatbot over the returns policy documents, since that is the established pattern for policy questions and lets the team start building immediately.
options.why: This jumps to a solution before discovery. The pattern may turn out to be right, but nothing yet shows that the problem is answering policy questions rather than, say, processing return requests.

options.text: Build a prototype on the strongest available model this week so the CIO can react to something concrete.
options.why: A demo before discovery anchors expectations on curated inputs and skips the questions that determine whether a chatbot is even the right shape.

options.text: Run structured discovery first: current process, volumes, error costs, data sources and their sensitivity, success metrics, constraints, and who decides.
options.why: Structured discovery establishes the facts that drive every later choice, including whether a chatbot is the right solution, what accuracy is needed and what data may be used.

options.text: Ask for the approved budget and timeline, then size a model and architecture that fits them.
options.why: Budget and timeline are constraints, but they say nothing about error costs, data, success criteria or decision rights, so an architecture sized to them alone is a guess.

explanation: Discovery comes before design. An architect gathers the current process, volumes, cost of errors, data sources and their sensitivity, measurable success criteria, constraints and decision rights before proposing a model or architecture. Prototyping or picking a pattern first is the classic jump-to-solution mistake.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

stem: During discovery for a claims-triage assistant at a health insurer, an architect has 20 minutes with the operations director. Triage volume is about 9,000 claims a week. Which question will most change the architecture the architect proposes?

options.text: What happens when a claim is routed to the wrong team today, and what does that cost?
options.why: The cost and consequence of an error decides the accuracy threshold, whether human review is needed and for which claims, and therefore whether a single classification call, a review queue or a richer workflow is appropriate.

options.text: Which Claude model does the operations team expect the solution to use?
options.why: Model choice follows from the requirements; asking the business to pick one first inverts the process and rarely produces useful information.

options.text: Should the assistant be delivered inside the existing claims portal, as a Microsoft Teams bot, or as a separate chat interface that agents open in a browser?
options.why: Delivery surface is a real question, but it affects the presentation layer, not the accuracy target, review strategy or data flow that shape the architecture.

options.text: How soon can a working demo be shown to the executive committee?
options.why: Demo timing is a project-management concern; it reveals nothing about the process, its error costs or what success looks like.

explanation: Among discovery questions, the cost of an error is the one that most shapes the design: it sets the acceptance threshold, determines where humans stay in the loop and justifies the spend on accuracy. Surface, model preference and demo dates are downstream of it.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria

stem: A public-sector benefits agency has finished a two-week discovery for an eligibility-question assistant and wants to move into design. Which two outputs should exist before design begins? (Choose two.)

options.text: A finalized system prompt agreed with the policy team.
options.why: The system prompt is a design and build artifact; writing it during discovery fixes an implementation before the requirements and success criteria are settled.

options.text: A documented current-state process with monthly volumes, turnaround times, and the frequency and cost of errors.
options.why: The current-state picture with volumes and error costs is the baseline that every later trade-off, including accuracy targets and review strategy, is measured against.

options.text: A chosen embedding model and chunk size for the policy corpus.
options.why: Chunking and embedding choices are retrieval design decisions that depend on the data and query patterns discovered; they are not discovery outputs.

options.text: A signed service-level agreement guaranteeing 99% correct answers.
options.why: Committing to an accuracy guarantee before anything has been measured over-promises on probabilistic output; SLA wording comes after a pilot has produced evidence.

options.text: Agreed, measurable success criteria with a baseline and the named person who will accept the result.
options.why: Specific, measurable, achievable and relevant criteria, plus a named decision-maker, are what let the team know when the design has succeeded and who says so.

options.text: A working demo the sponsor can share with the wider department.
options.why: A demo before design invites the department to treat curated examples as the product and drives expectations ahead of any measurement.

explanation: Discovery should end with an agreed picture of the current process (volumes, timings, error costs) and measurable success criteria with a baseline and an accountable decision-maker. Prompts, retrieval parameters, SLAs and demos all belong to later phases.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria

stem: A SaaS company's support VP wants a Claude assistant to resolve tickets with no agent involvement; legal wants a human to review every reply; finance has capped monthly spend. Discovery shows 68% of tickets are password and billing FAQs with negligible error cost, 20% are how-to questions, and 12% are contract disputes where a wrong reply has averaged $1,800 in credits. Which approach best reconciles the stakeholders?

options.text: Adopt legal's requirement to review every reply, because compliance requirements always take precedence over efficiency goals and the other stakeholders will accept that reasoning.
options.why: Reviewing every reply spends human time on the 68% of tickets where an error costs almost nothing, which defeats the efficiency case and breaches the finance cap for no risk benefit.

options.text: Adopt the support VP's requirement, because the sponsor who funds the project holds the decision rights.
options.why: Decision rights let the sponsor choose among options, not ignore a $1,800-per-error category; full automation of contract disputes is the risk legal is right to reject.

options.text: Propose the highest-accuracy model tier so that the assistant is reliable enough for every category and no review is needed.
options.why: A stronger model lowers the error rate but cannot eliminate it; on high-cost disputes the residual errors still need a human, and the tier raises spend across all tickets.

options.text: Segment by error cost: auto-resolve the FAQ categories, send contract disputes to human review, and confirm the split with the sponsor and legal.
options.why: Segmenting by the discovered error cost satisfies efficiency where errors are cheap, keeps review where they are expensive, fits the spend cap, and makes the decision explicit for the people who hold it.

explanation: Discovery data about error cost by segment resolves conflicting stakeholder positions better than picking a winner: automate where errors are cheap, keep humans where they are expensive, and record who agreed. A bigger model is not a substitute for a review decision.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

stem: An architect at a bank is scoping a Claude summarizer for contact-centre call notes. Late in discovery, an analyst mentions that the notes often contain full card numbers and account balances. The compliance owner has not attended any session, and the workshop is due to close with an architecture proposal tomorrow. What should the architect do?

options.text: Proceed with the proposal and list PII redaction as an implementation detail for the build team to handle.
options.why: Whether card data may leave the bank's boundary at all is a requirement that shapes the architecture; treating it as a build detail risks designing something compliance will later reject.

options.text: Extend discovery to classify the data's sensitivity with the compliance owner, and establish which data may leave the bank's boundary and who signs off, before proposing an architecture.
options.why: Data sensitivity and decision rights are discovery outputs. Getting the compliance owner's classification and sign-off criteria first prevents a proposal built on an unapproved data flow.

options.text: Drop the call-notes source from scope so the proposal can be delivered on time, and revisit it after launch.
options.why: The call notes are the input the summarizer exists to process; removing them meets the date by removing the use case, and defers the same question to a worse moment.

options.text: Rely on the API provider's data-retention terms to satisfy compliance and keep the proposal date.
options.why: Provider terms are one input to a compliance decision, not the decision; the bank's own owner must classify the data and decide what may be sent.

explanation: Discovery must surface data sources and their sensitivity and identify who has authority over them. A late finding of card data is a reason to extend discovery and bring in the missing stakeholder, not to guess, defer or scope the data away.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

stem: An insurer's COO tells the architect that a Claude document-extraction system must be "99% accurate" before she will fund it. Today clerks key the same fields manually in about 20 minutes per document; nobody has ever measured the clerks' error rate, and the extraction covers 30 fields of very different importance. The COO wants a number in next week's proposal. What should the architect propose?

options.text: Measure the clerks' current error rate on a sample first, then set a per-field target weighted by the cost of each error, to be confirmed in a pilot.
options.why: An achievable, relevant criterion is anchored on a measured baseline and on what each error costs; a blanket 99% across 30 unequal fields is neither. The pilot then validates the number with evidence.

options.text: Accept the 99% target and commit to it in the proposal, since Claude models routinely exceed that on extraction benchmarks.
options.why: Benchmarks are not this insurer's documents, and committing to a figure with no baseline over-promises on probabilistic output before anything has been measured.

options.text: Counter with 95%, which is a typical figure for document extraction, and put it in the proposal as the acceptance criterion.
options.why: A generic figure is as arbitrary as 99%; it is not tied to the manual baseline or to which fields matter, so it cannot be defended when the pilot reports results.

options.text: Explain that no accuracy figure can responsibly be set until the system has been built and measured on real documents, so the proposal should leave the criterion open.
options.why: Leaving the criterion open leaves the sponsor with nothing to fund against; a baseline measurement and a cost-weighted target can be proposed before any system is built.

explanation: Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant. With no baseline, the architect's job is to create one (measure the current manual process), weight the target by error cost per field, and treat the pilot as the validation step, rather than accepting, haggling over or refusing a number.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria

stem: An architect must present a model-tier decision for an invoice-processing pipeline to a CFO and a COO, neither of whom is technical. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: A comparison table of benchmark scores, context-window sizes, output tokens per second and knowledge-cutoff dates for each candidate model tier.
options.why: Technical specifications do not tell a CFO or COO what the choice means for their invoices, spend or exposure; the audience cannot act on them.

options.text: Cost per invoice, turnaround time, expected error rate and the cost of an error for two or three options, with a recommendation.
options.why: Translating accuracy, cost and latency into business terms, showing the options, and stating a recommendation is what lets executives fund and approve the decision.

options.text: Only the recommended option, presented as the obvious choice, so that the executives are not confused by alternatives.
options.why: Hiding the alternatives hides the trade-offs; executives cannot approve a trade-off they have not seen, and the decision will be reopened later.

options.text: A live demo of the strongest model on a few sample invoices, so the executives can judge the quality themselves.
options.why: A handful of curated invoices shows feasibility, not the error rate or cost at volume, and invites the executives to treat the demo as the decision.

explanation: Architectural decisions are communicated to funders in business terms: what each option costs, how fast it is, how often it is wrong and what a wrong answer costs, followed by a clear recommendation. Specifications and demos do not give decision-makers what they need.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

stem: Eight months ago a logistics company's architect chose a fixed prompt-chain workflow rather than an autonomous agent for shipment-exception handling. That architect has since left. A new technical lead wants to "upgrade to agents", and nobody can explain what constraints drove the original choice. Which practice would have prevented this situation?

options.text: Pinning the decision thread in the team's chat channel so it stayed discoverable.
options.why: Chat threads mix the decision with noise, lack a stable structure and are rarely found by people who join later; they are not a record.

options.text: Explaining the reasoning in comments at the top of the orchestration code.
options.why: Code comments capture local implementation notes, not the business context, options considered and consequences; they also drift as the code changes.

options.text: Presenting the decision to the steering committee with a slide on the rejected alternatives, so that the leadership team could recall it later.
options.why: A presentation communicates the decision at the time but does not preserve it; slides are not maintained with the system and memories fade.

options.text: Recording an architecture decision record with the context, options, decision and consequences, kept with the project.
options.why: An ADR captures why a decision was made, what was rejected and what it costs, and lives alongside the system so later teams can revisit it deliberately rather than guess.

explanation: Architecture decision records preserve the context, options considered, decision and consequences so that future teams can understand and, if the context changes, deliberately supersede a decision. Chat, comments and slides do not survive staff turnover.
reference: General architecture practice — Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

stem: An architect is preparing a steering-committee presentation recommending a Claude-based product-description generator for a retailer's 40,000-SKU catalogue. Which two elements should the presentation include? (Choose two.)

options.text: The options considered and the trade-off each makes between accuracy, cost, latency and risk, expressed in business terms.
options.why: Decision-makers need to see the alternatives and what each trades away; that is what makes the recommendation defensible and the approval informed.

options.text: Only the recommended option, to keep the committee focused on approving the budget.
options.why: Suppressing the alternatives hides the trade-offs the committee is being asked to accept; it may speed approval but undermines trust when the trade-offs surface later.

options.text: A statement that the system prompt prevents the model from producing incorrect product claims.
options.why: A prompt reduces but cannot eliminate errors; presenting it as a guarantee over-promises and sets the committee up for surprise when descriptions need correction.

options.text: The residual risks after mitigation, such as the expected rate of descriptions needing correction, and who is accountable for them.
options.why: Naming the residual risk, its expected rate and its owner lets the committee decide with eyes open and prevents the trade-off from being hidden.

options.text: Demo outputs from a curated set of ten products, presented as representative of production quality.
options.why: Ten hand-picked outputs show feasibility, not quality across 40,000 SKUs; presenting them as representative misleads the committee about the error rate.

options.text: The full system prompt, so the committee can review the wording line by line.
options.why: Prompt wording is an implementation detail the committee cannot evaluate; it displaces the business trade-offs the presentation should be about.

explanation: Communicating an architectural decision means showing the options and their trade-offs in business terms, and being explicit about residual risk and ownership. Hiding alternatives, promising that prompts prevent errors and passing off curated demos as production quality are the common ways such presentations mislead.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

stem: A telecom's architect ran a 500-case held-out evaluation of two model tiers for classifying 200,000 monthly service requests. The larger tier scored 94% and would cost about $30,000 more per month; the smaller tier scored 91%. Operations data puts the cost of a misrouted request at about $40. How should the architect communicate the decision to the steering committee?

options.text: Recommend the smaller tier, since a three-point difference is within normal evaluation noise and the savings are certain.
options.why: Three points on 500 cases is a real difference, and at 200,000 requests it represents about 6,000 misroutes a month; calling it noise hides the trade-off rather than communicating it.

options.text: Recommend the larger tier because it is the most capable model available, and capability reduces risk.
options.why: The conclusion happens to be right, but the reasoning is not: the committee needs the business case, not an appeal to capability, or the same argument will justify any spend.

options.text: Show both options with the cost of errors: roughly 6,000 extra misroutes at $40 each is about $240,000 a month, which outweighs the $30,000, then state the assumptions to validate.
options.why: Converting the accuracy gap into error cost at real volume makes the trade-off legible, supports a recommendation, and exposes the assumptions (error cost, volume) the committee can challenge.

options.text: Present both options without a recommendation and let the committee weigh the numbers, since it holds the decision rights.
options.why: Decision rights belong to the committee, but the architect is paid for a recommendation; presenting numbers without one abdicates the role and slows the decision.

explanation: Trade-offs are communicated by converting technical metrics into business consequences: accuracy difference times volume times error cost, compared with the cost difference. State the options, the recommendation and the assumptions behind it so stakeholders can approve or challenge them.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria

stem: An architect recommends that a Claude underwriting assistant at an insurer route 15% of cases to a human reviewer. The CTO objects: "If we need reviewers, it looks like the AI doesn't work; take it out." Evaluation shows the 15% are the cases where the model's accuracy is lowest and the cost of an error is highest. What is the architect's best response?

options.text: Reframe review as risk management: show the error cost concentrated in those cases and offer the review rate as a dial with published criteria for lowering it.
options.why: This keeps the trade-off visible, ties the review step to measured risk rather than to doubt about the AI, and gives the CTO a path to reduce it based on evidence.

options.text: Remove the review step as the CTO asks, since the CTO holds the decision rights for the project, and rely on post-launch monitoring and customer complaints to reveal any problems.
options.why: Decision rights do not remove the architect's duty to make the risk explicit; dropping review on the highest-cost cases without a stated trade-off hides the consequence from the person deciding.

options.text: Keep the review step but strengthen the system prompt with instructions that the model must be accurate on underwriting cases.
options.why: Instructing a model to be accurate does not change its accuracy; it neither answers the CTO's objection nor changes the measured risk.

options.text: Promise that the review step can be removed once the model has been fine-tuned to 100% on those cases.
options.why: Promising 100% on the hardest cases over-promises on probabilistic output and sets an expectation that will be missed.

explanation: Stakeholder objections to human review are answered by reframing the step in business terms: the review rate targets measured error cost, and it can be lowered as evidence accumulates. Capitulating, prompt pleading and promising perfection all hide or misstate the trade-off.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

stem: A pharmaceutical company must answer regulator queries about adverse-event reports under a rule that takes effect in 10 weeks. Discovery set the acceptance criterion at 92% correct on an agreed test set. The architect has three options: prompt engineering alone (88% today, two more weeks), adding retrieval over the internal safety database (estimated 93%, eight weeks), or an agentic system with tools (estimated 95%, sixteen weeks, higher operating cost). Which recommendation should the architect put to the sponsor?

options.text: The agentic option, because the highest accuracy is the safest choice under regulatory scrutiny and the deadline can be negotiated.
options.why: It misses a fixed regulatory date by six weeks and adds complexity and cost beyond what the agreed criterion needs; assuming the deadline moves is not a recommendation the sponsor can act on.

options.text: The retrieval option, presented alongside the other two, as the simplest path that meets the criterion inside the deadline, with the agentic option held as a later iteration if measurement shows it is needed.
options.why: It satisfies the agreed criterion and the hard deadline with the least complexity, shows the sponsor the alternatives, and reserves added complexity for when evidence justifies it.

options.text: The prompt-engineering option, delivered early, with a commitment to close the four-point gap through further tuning before the deadline.
options.why: It ships below the criterion on a promise; committing to close a measured gap by tuning alone over-promises and gives the sponsor no evidence.

options.text: The agentic option, with two parallel teams to compress the sixteen weeks to ten, since it best serves the long-term roadmap.
options.why: Compressing a sixteen-week build by doubling teams is a schedule gamble on the most complex option, when a simpler one already meets the criterion on time.

explanation: Recommend the simplest option that meets the agreed criteria within the constraints, present the alternatives and their trade-offs, and add complexity only when measurement shows it improves outcomes. A hard deadline and an agreed threshold are the discriminators here.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (find the simplest solution possible)

stem: A hospital's chief nursing officer asks the architect: "Can you guarantee the discharge-summary assistant will never produce a wrong statement?" How should the architect respond?

options.text: Yes, provided the system prompt instructs the model to state only facts that appear in the patient's chart and to refuse to write anything it cannot cite from the record.
options.why: Prompt instructions reduce errors but cannot guarantee their absence; answering yes over-promises on probabilistic output in a clinical setting.

options.text: Yes, by setting the sampling temperature to zero so the output is deterministic.
options.why: Temperature affects randomness, not correctness; a deterministic wrong statement is still a wrong statement.

options.text: No; output is probabilistic, so propose measurable acceptance criteria, review of high-risk content and a pilot to measure the real error rate.
options.why: Being honest that errors will occur, then agreeing how to measure and contain them, aligns expectations with what the system can actually deliver.

options.text: No, and recommend the hospital not proceed, because clinical documentation cannot tolerate any error.
options.why: Human-written summaries also contain errors; the question is whether measured error rates with review are acceptable, which a pilot can answer.

explanation: Expectation alignment starts with the fact that LLM output is probabilistic: no configuration guarantees zero errors. The architect replaces a guarantee with measurable acceptance criteria, a review strategy for high-risk content and a pilot that produces real evidence.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria

stem: A legal-tech vendor is drafting a contract for a Claude-based contract-review service. The draft SLA reads: "The service will be available 99.9% of the time and will be 99.9% accurate." The architect is asked to review the clause. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep availability and latency as uptime-style SLOs, and state answer quality separately as a measured target on an agreed sample with a defined method and review cadence.
options.why: Availability can be monitored continuously and guaranteed; answer quality can only be measured on a sample by an agreed method, so the two need different wording and different remedies.

options.text: Lower the accuracy figure to 99%, which is achievable with a strong model and careful prompting.
options.why: Changing the number keeps the mistake: an accuracy guarantee written like an uptime guarantee has no agreed measurement method, sample or cadence behind it.

options.text: Remove all quality language from the contract, since model output cannot be measured reliably.
options.why: Quality can be measured on an agreed evaluation set; leaving it out entirely leaves the customer with no expectation and the vendor with no defined obligation.

options.text: Keep the clause as written, because availability and accuracy are both percentages and can be monitored together.
options.why: They are not measured the same way: availability is observed on every request, while accuracy needs graded samples; conflating them makes the accuracy clause unenforceable and over-promised.

explanation: SLA wording for LLM services separates availability and latency (continuously observable, uptime-style commitments) from answer quality (a target measured on an agreed sample by a defined method at a defined cadence). Treating accuracy like uptime over-promises and cannot be honoured.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

stem: A university is piloting a Claude assistant that answers student questions about enrolment and financial aid. The registrar wants a feedback loop with stakeholders during the eight-week pilot. Which two practices make the loop effective? (Choose two.)

options.text: Collect all feedback in a survey at the end of the pilot so the results are not biased by early problems.
options.why: An end-of-pilot survey is too late to act on; the pilot's value comes from finding and fixing problems while it runs.

options.text: Hold a weekly review of a stratified sample of conversations with the registrar's staff, classify errors, and add failures to the evaluation set.
options.why: A fixed cadence, a representative sample, an error taxonomy and a growing evaluation set turn stakeholder feedback into measurable improvement.

options.text: Have the model rate its own answers for correctness and use that score as the primary feedback signal.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of correctness and does not involve the stakeholders whose expectations the loop is meant to align.

options.text: Capture in-product flags from students and staff, route them to a triage queue, and report the trend by category at each review.
options.why: In-product flags give continuous, low-friction signal from real users, and reporting them by category at the review keeps stakeholders informed of what is and is not improving.

options.text: Change the system prompt immediately after each complaint so stakeholders see fast responsiveness.
options.why: Reacting to single complaints without measurement produces churn and regressions; changes should follow the reviewed evidence and pass the evaluation set.

explanation: An effective feedback loop has a cadence, a representative sample, a way to classify errors, a channel for real users to flag problems, and an evaluation set that grows with the failures found. End-of-pilot surveys, model self-ratings and reflexive prompt edits are the usual failure modes.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Develop test cases

stem: A mortgage lender is four weeks into a twelve-week pilot of a Claude document-checking assistant with a cohort of 25 processors. The sponsoring VP, impressed by a demo, forwards the link to all 300 processors and starts asking for three new document types to be added. What should the architect do?

options.text: Welcome the wider use, since 300 users will generate far more feedback than 25 and the pilot can be shortened accordingly, and add the three document types to the current scope.
options.why: Expanding the cohort and the scope mid-pilot invalidates the measurement plan, spreads support thin and turns the pilot into an unmanaged launch.

options.text: Declare the pilot complete and move to launch, since the sponsor has decided the system works.
options.why: A sponsor's enthusiasm after a demo is not the agreed exit criterion; treating a demo as a launch skips the measurement the pilot exists to produce.

options.text: Pause the pilot until the sponsor agrees in writing not to expand it again.
options.why: Stopping the pilot punishes the team for the sponsor's enthusiasm and loses momentum; the aim is to re-anchor expectations, not to stall.

options.text: Re-anchor on the pilot charter: restore the agreed cohort, restate the success and exit criteria, and log the new document types for the next iteration.
options.why: The charter is the shared agreement on scope, cohort and exit criteria; returning to it keeps the measurement valid while the new requests are captured rather than refused.

explanation: Expectation management during a pilot means holding to the agreed charter: scope, cohort, success and exit criteria. Scope creep and a demo being treated as a launch are handled by re-anchoring on that agreement and routing new requests into the iteration backlog.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

stem: A pilot of a Claude claims-coding assistant at a health system ended at 91% field-level accuracy against an agreed 95% acceptance criterion. The sponsor wants to launch anyway to hit a quarterly goal. Which response best manages expectations?

options.text: Decline to support the launch and escalate to the CIO, since the acceptance criterion was not met.
options.why: The sponsor holds the decision rights; the architect's job is to make the gap and the options clear, not to veto or go over the sponsor's head as a first move.

options.text: Present the gap with the error breakdown and its financial impact, then offer options such as launching only the claim types already above 95%, extending the pilot, or launching with a higher review rate, with a recommendation.
options.why: This respects the sponsor's decision rights while keeping the trade-off explicit: each option states what is gained and what risk is accepted.

options.text: Launch as requested and report the 91% as 'on track' so that the quarterly goal is not jeopardized.
options.why: Misreporting a missed criterion hides the trade-off from the people who own the risk and destroys the credibility of every later metric.

options.text: Lower the acceptance criterion to 90% so that the pilot can be recorded as successful.
options.why: Moving the goalposts after the result is known makes the criterion meaningless; if 95% was wrong, that should be argued from error cost, not from the quarterly calendar.

explanation: When a pilot misses its criterion, the architect keeps the trade-off visible: show the gap and its impact, offer options that trade scope, time or review effort against risk, and recommend one, leaving the decision with the sponsor. Hiding the gap or rewriting the criterion breaks expectation alignment.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

stem: An enterprise customer wants a contract for a Claude-based procurement-query service with 99.5% availability, p95 latency under 3 seconds, at least 97% correct answers, and financial penalties. The service depends on a third-party model API, and the current evaluation shows 96.2% correct on 400 cases with a confidence interval of roughly ±2 points. Which three elements should the architect insist the SLA contain? (Choose three.)

options.text: Availability and latency as service-level objectives with explicit carve-outs for the upstream model API's own availability.
options.why: Uptime-style objectives are appropriate for availability and latency, but the vendor cannot commit beyond what its upstream dependency commits to, so the carve-out must be explicit.

options.text: A 97% accuracy guarantee, since the current 96.2% is within two points and improvement is expected.
options.why: Committing to a figure the current measurement does not support, on a sample whose confidence interval spans the target, over-promises and invites penalties for statistical noise.

options.text: Answer quality as a measured target on a versioned, jointly agreed evaluation set, with the sample size, grading method and review cadence written into the contract.
options.why: Quality can only be measured by an agreed method on an agreed set; writing the method, sample and cadence into the contract makes the target meaningful and disputes resolvable.

options.text: A reduced evaluation set of the clearest cases so that the measured figure comfortably exceeds 97%.
options.why: Gaming the sample produces a number that does not reflect production traffic and will be exposed the first time the customer measures independently.

options.text: A remediation process for quality shortfalls, such as root-cause review and a fix window, rather than uptime-style penalties on answer quality.
options.why: Quality on probabilistic output is improved through diagnosis and iteration; a defined remediation path aligns both parties on what happens when the target is missed.

options.text: No quality commitments at all, on the grounds that model outputs are probabilistic.
options.why: Probabilistic does not mean unmeasurable; refusing any quality commitment leaves the customer without an expectation and is unlikely to be accepted.

explanation: An SLA for an LLM service commits to availability and latency as observable objectives (net of upstream dependencies), states answer quality as a target measured on a versioned, agreed evaluation set with a defined method and cadence, and pairs quality shortfalls with a remediation process. Guaranteeing a figure the evidence does not support, or gaming the sample, are the over-promising traps.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Define your success criteria; Develop test cases

stem: An architect is handing a Claude-based order-status assistant to a retailer's operations team. The package contains a C4 container diagram and the repository. The operations lead asks what is missing before her team can be on call for it. Which addition matters most?

options.text: A runbook: known failure modes, diagnostic steps, escalation paths and how to roll back a prompt or model version.
options.why: An on-call team needs to know what can go wrong, how to recognise it and what to do; a runbook is the document that turns a diagram and code into something operable.

options.text: The slide deck used for the executive demo, so the team understands the business case.
options.why: The business case helps context but does not tell anyone what to do at 2 a.m. when the assistant starts returning errors.

options.text: The raw evaluation dataset, without the scoring method or thresholds, so the team can read example inputs and outputs and form its own view of quality.
options.why: Evaluation data is part of a good handoff, but without the method and thresholds it does not support operations, and it does not address on-call readiness.

options.text: The vendor's published benchmark scores for the chosen model tier.
options.why: Benchmark scores say nothing about how this system fails or how to recover it.

explanation: A handoff package includes the architecture diagram, prompt and schema versions, evaluation results, a cost model, ownership, and a runbook. For an on-call team the runbook is the essential piece: failure modes, diagnostics, escalation and rollback.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

stem: An architect produced a single diagram of a Claude-powered employee-onboarding system with 40 boxes covering every function, queue and database. Executives say they cannot follow it; engineers say it still omits the retry and routing logic they need. What should the architect do?

options.text: Add the retry and routing detail to the same diagram, with colour coding and a legend, so that it becomes the single complete reference for every audience.
options.why: One diagram cannot serve both audiences; adding detail makes it less readable for executives without becoming a proper engineering view.

options.text: Remove the technical detail and keep one simplified diagram for everyone.
options.why: Simplifying loses the detail engineers need to build and operate the system; the executives' view and the engineers' view are different documents.

options.text: Produce layered views: a context diagram for executives, and container and component diagrams with the flow detail for engineers.
options.why: C4-style layering gives each audience a view at the right altitude, from system context down to components and flows, without overloading any single picture.

options.text: Replace the diagram with a written description of the system, since prose is easier to read at both levels.
options.why: Prose does not fix the audience mismatch and is harder to scan for structure; diagrams at appropriate levels are the standard tool.

explanation: Architecture documentation is layered by audience: a system-context view for sponsors and executives, container and component views for engineers, and sequence or flow views where the logic matters. One diagram for everyone satisfies no one.
reference: General architecture practice — C4 model (context, container, component)

stem: A fintech's platform team is preparing to hand a Claude transaction-categorization service to a maintenance team. Which two practices ensure the prompts and outputs are documented well enough to be maintained? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep prompts in version control with a changelog, and attach the evaluation results obtained with each version.
options.why: Versioned prompts with their evaluation results let maintainers see what changed, why, and what it did to quality, and give them something to roll back to.

options.text: Store the production prompt in a shared document that any team member can edit as issues arise.
options.why: An editable shared document has no version history tied to deployments or evaluations, so nobody can tell which wording is live or what a change did.

options.text: Rely on the model to remember which prompt version it is running so that no separate record is needed.
options.why: The model has no memory of deployments; the version must be recorded by the application and its logs.

options.text: Tune the prompt directly in the production console when categories change, since that is the fastest path.
options.why: Live edits bypass evaluation and versioning; they are how undocumented regressions enter production.

options.text: Document the output schema with a version number and list the downstream consumers that depend on each field.
options.why: Downstream systems depend on the output contract; a versioned schema with known consumers lets maintainers change it safely and assess the impact of a change.

explanation: Maintainable documentation treats prompts and output schemas as versioned artifacts: prompts in version control with evaluation results per version, and schemas with version numbers and a list of consumers. Shared editable docs and live console edits leave no usable record.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

stem: A government agency has approved an architect's design for a Claude-based permit-application assistant and assigned implementation to a separate contractor. The design document says "use Claude with retrieval over the regulations and well-crafted prompts." The contractor's lead asks for implementation guidance. What should the architect provide?

options.text: The proof-of-concept notebook, so the contractor can extend working code rather than reading documents.
options.why: A notebook shows one way something once worked; it carries no contracts, thresholds or constraints, so the contractor will inherit its shortcuts as requirements.

options.text: Interface contracts for inputs and outputs, the evaluation harness with acceptance thresholds, latency and cost budgets, the constraints and decisions already made, and who owns each part.
options.why: Implementation guidance turns a design into something buildable and testable: what the components must accept and produce, how success is measured, the non-functional budgets, the decisions not to reopen, and ownership.

options.text: A standing daily call for the contractor to ask questions, in place of written guidance that would go stale.
options.why: Conversations do not scale and leave no record; the contractor will make undocumented assumptions between calls and the agency cannot verify the result.

options.text: The complete implementation written by the architect, since only the designer can ensure fidelity to the design.
options.why: Building it personally defeats the assignment and does not produce guidance others could follow; the architect's role is to make the design implementable by others.

explanation: Implementation guidance makes a design buildable by another team: interface contracts, the evaluation harness and acceptance thresholds, non-functional budgets, recorded decisions and constraints, and ownership. A phrase like "well-crafted prompts" is not guidance.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Develop test cases

stem: At 2 a.m. an on-call engineer at an e-commerce company is paged: a Claude product-tagging service has been returning malformed JSON on 5% of requests since the previous afternoon, and downstream jobs are failing. The engineer finds the architecture diagram and the decision records but spends three hours before discovering that a prompt change was deployed at 4 p.m. Which documentation gap most directly caused the long recovery?

options.text: The architecture diagram did not show the downstream jobs that consume the tagging output, so the engineer could not see the blast radius of the failure quickly enough.
options.why: Knowing the blast radius helps prioritise, but the engineer already knew jobs were failing; it does not shorten the search for the cause.

options.text: The decision records did not explain why JSON was chosen as the output format.
options.why: The rationale for the format is irrelevant to diagnosing why the format broke yesterday afternoon.

options.text: The evaluation dataset was not included in the handoff package.
options.why: An evaluation set helps confirm a fix, but it would not have pointed the engineer at the 4 p.m. prompt deployment.

options.text: No runbook mapped the symptom to diagnostic steps, no record showed the deployed prompt version, and no rollback procedure existed.
options.why: A runbook entry for malformed output that says "check the deployed prompt version and roll back" would have resolved the incident in minutes; the missing operational documentation is the gap.

explanation: Diagrams and decision records explain the system; runbooks and version records let people operate it. Incident recovery depends on symptom-to-action guidance, a record of which prompt and model version is live, and a tested rollback path.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

stem: A consultancy is handing a Claude-based loan-document assistant to a bank. The sponsor requires predictable monthly cost, internal audit requires the bank to show which prompt and model produced any given output, and the on-call team requires recovery within 30 minutes of a bad change. Which three items in the handoff package satisfy all three requirements together? (Choose three.)

options.text: A prompt and schema registry with version identifiers, and request logging that records the prompt and model version used for each output.
options.why: Version identifiers logged per request are what let audit trace any output to the exact prompt and model, and they are also what a rollback targets.

options.text: A detailed sequence diagram of every request path so that auditors can follow the logic.
options.why: Sequence diagrams explain behaviour but do not show which version produced a specific output; audit needs traceability, not logic walkthroughs.

options.text: A cost model that ties token usage per request type to expected volumes, with alert thresholds when spend departs from the range.
options.why: The sponsor's cost predictability comes from a model that forecasts spend from volume and flags departures early, not from a one-off estimate.

options.text: A summary of the vendor's model benchmark results as evidence of expected quality.
options.why: Benchmark summaries address none of the three requirements: they are not cost, traceability or recovery.

options.text: The full discovery transcripts so that the bank can reconstruct the original requirements.
options.why: Raw transcripts are not usable documentation; the agreed requirements and decisions belong in the design document and ADRs, and they do not help cost, audit or recovery.

options.text: A runbook with a tested rollback procedure for prompt and model versions, and a RACI naming the owner of each.
options.why: A 30-minute recovery target requires a rehearsed rollback and a named owner who can execute it; without both, the on-call team cannot meet the requirement.

explanation: A complete handoff package matches documentation to the stakeholders who depend on it: a cost model for the sponsor, versioned prompt and schema records with per-request logging for audit, and a runbook with tested rollback and named owners for operations. Diagrams, benchmarks and transcripts do not meet those needs.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

stem: A regional utility's product owner has seen a convincing demo of a Claude outage-communication assistant on 15 hand-picked examples and wants to launch it to all customers next week, skipping the planned pilot. Why is the pilot still needed?

options.text: Because the demo used an older model version and the results must be regenerated.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario says the model version differs; and regenerating a demo would still be a demo.

options.text: Because launches require a security review, which the pilot phase is intended to satisfy.
options.why: A security review may well be required, but it is a separate gate; the pilot's purpose is measurement on real traffic.

options.text: Because the demo ran without a system prompt, so its outputs do not reflect the intended design.
options.why: The scenario gives no reason to think the demo was misconfigured; the objection to skipping a pilot holds even for a perfectly configured demo.

options.text: Because a demo shows feasibility on curated inputs, while a pilot measures the agreed success criteria on real traffic with a feedback loop before launch.
options.why: Fifteen hand-picked examples cannot reveal the error rate, edge cases or user reaction at scale; the pilot is where those are measured against the criteria before customers are exposed.

explanation: In the lifecycle, a demo demonstrates feasibility and a pilot produces evidence: measured performance against success criteria on real inputs, with a feedback loop, before launch. Treating a demo as a launch is a recurring failure pattern.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)

stem: A travel company runs a Claude itinerary assistant in production. The model provider announces that the model version in use will be retired in six months. How should the architect handle this?

options.text: Treat it as a change: run the evaluation suite against the successor model, compare, record the decision, and roll out in stages with a rollback path.
options.why: A model change can alter behaviour; managing it like any other change, with evaluation evidence, a recorded decision and a staged rollout, keeps quality and accountability intact.

options.text: Update the model identifier on the retirement date, since prompts written for one Claude model behave the same on its successor and the evaluation suite has already been passed once.
options.why: Successor models can respond differently to the same prompts; swapping without re-evaluation risks a regression on the day there is no fallback.

options.text: Freeze the current model by declining the upgrade, since a working production system should not be changed.
options.why: A retired model stops being available; refusing to plan the migration only removes the six months in which to do it safely.

options.text: Ask the provider for an exception, since the system was designed and accepted on the current version.
options.why: Deprecation timelines are not usually negotiable per customer, and relying on an exception leaves the system without a plan.

explanation: Model deprecation is change management: evaluate the replacement against the existing test suite, record the decision (an ADR), roll out in stages with monitoring and a rollback path, and communicate to stakeholders. Blind swaps and refusal to migrate are both failures of lifecycle support.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Develop test cases

stem: A property insurer's Claude claims-summary service has been in production for three months after handoff. The architect is defining how the monitoring phase feeds the iteration phase. Which two practices are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Track the average output length per request as a proxy for summary quality.
options.why: Length is easy to measure but says nothing about whether summaries are correct; it is a proxy that will be optimised instead of quality.

options.text: Open a new iteration whenever the model vendor publishes a newer model.
options.why: Iteration should be driven by measured need, not by vendor releases; a new model is a candidate to evaluate, not a trigger by itself.

options.text: Sample production outputs for human review on a fixed cadence and compare the measured accuracy against the pilot baseline.
options.why: Ongoing sampled review against the accepted baseline is how drift is detected; without it the team has no idea whether quality is holding.

options.text: Count the number of prompt edits per month as the key health indicator.
options.why: Edit frequency measures activity, not outcome; a stable prompt and a degrading system would look healthy.

options.text: Define thresholds, such as accuracy drift or an escalation-rate rise, that trigger an iteration cycle, and add the failing cases to the evaluation set.
options.why: Explicit triggers make the monitoring-to-iteration handover deliberate, and feeding production failures into the evaluation set means each iteration is tested against what actually went wrong.

explanation: Monitoring feeds iteration through sampled human review against the accepted baseline, explicit thresholds that open an iteration, and an evaluation set that grows with production failures. Length, edit counts and vendor release calendars are not quality signals.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Develop test cases

stem: A support lead at a software company, responding to a complaint about tone, edited the production system prompt of a Claude ticket-triage assistant directly. The next day, category-extraction accuracy fell from 96% to 88%, and the on-call team took a day to connect the two events. Which change best prevents a recurrence?

options.text: Revert the edit and instruct the support lead to route future wording requests through the architect.
options.why: This fixes the instance, not the cause; the next well-meaning edit by anyone with access will do the same thing.

options.text: Put prompts under the same change management as code: versioned, gated by the evaluation suite before deployment, rolled out in stages, with a rollback path and no direct production edits.
options.why: Treating prompt changes as releases means the evaluation suite would have caught the 8-point drop before deployment, the version record would have linked the events, and rollback would have been immediate.

options.text: Add explicit accuracy and tone requirements to the system prompt so that future edits cannot trade one for the other.
options.why: Prompt text cannot enforce its own preservation; the problem is an unmanaged change process, not missing wording.

options.text: Move to a larger model tier so that wording changes have less effect on extraction accuracy.
options.why: A bigger model is not a change-control mechanism; unreviewed edits would still reach production unmeasured.

explanation: Prompt versioning is change management. Prompts are versioned artifacts that pass the evaluation suite before release, ship in stages, and can be rolled back; direct production edits are prohibited. That is what turns a day-long mystery into a caught regression.
reference: Claude Developer Platform docs — Develop test cases

stem: Two months after launching a Claude refund assistant, a marketplace's error taxonomy shows that 60% of errors come from cases where the refund policy itself is ambiguous, 25% from retrieval returning the wrong policy section, and 15% from formatting. The engineering team proposes rebuilding the system as a multi-tool agent. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Approve the rebuild, since an agent with tools can investigate ambiguous policy cases, retrieve the right section on its own and fix the formatting as a side effect, resolving all three error categories at once.
options.why: An agent cannot resolve a policy that is ambiguous to humans, and the rebuild adds cost and unpredictability without evidence that it addresses the measured failures.

options.text: Switch to a larger model tier first, since most errors stem from reasoning about ambiguous policy.
options.why: No model can reliably reason its way to the intended answer when the policy text itself does not define one; the fix belongs with the policy owners.

options.text: Fix the largest measured failure first by clarifying the policy with its owners and improving retrieval, re-measure, and add complexity only if the evaluation shows it is needed.
options.why: Iteration should target the measured causes in order of impact, then re-measure; adding architectural complexity is justified only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.

options.text: Fix the formatting errors first, since they are the cheapest to resolve and show quick progress.
options.why: Formatting is 15% of errors; starting there optimises for visible activity rather than impact.

explanation: The iteration phase works from the error taxonomy: address the largest measured cause first (here, an ambiguous policy, which is a stakeholder and data fix, not a model fix), re-measure, and only then consider more complex architecture. Start simple and add complexity only when measurement shows it helps.
reference: Anthropic — Building effective agents (add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes)

stem: A bank runs three Claude-based systems built by different teams, and each reached production by a different route: one after an executive demo, one after a pilot with no exit criteria, one after a full evaluation. A new AI platform lead wants a single lifecycle standard with gates between phases. Which set of gate criteria is most sound?

options.text: Design to pilot needs agreed success criteria, an evaluation set and a named cohort; pilot to handoff needs the criteria met on real traffic, runbooks and named owners; monitoring opens iteration when measured thresholds are crossed.
options.why: Each gate is tied to evidence and artifacts appropriate to the phase: criteria and a test set before piloting, measured results plus operability before handoff, and explicit thresholds to trigger iteration.

options.text: Each gate is passed when the executive sponsor approves a demo, since sponsors hold the decision rights for their systems and a standard should respect that authority.
options.why: Sponsors decide, but a demo is not evidence; this standardises the treat-a-demo-as-a-launch failure the platform lead is trying to eliminate.

options.text: Design to pilot requires all planned features to be built; pilot to handoff requires the team to report confidence; iteration begins whenever users request new features.
options.why: Feature completeness, self-reported confidence and feature requests are not measurements; none of these gates asks whether the system meets its criteria.

options.text: Every gate requires a full security review and a model upgrade to the latest version, so that systems never fall behind and always pass with the newest capabilities.
options.why: Security review belongs in the lifecycle, but forcing a model upgrade at every gate injects unmeasured change at exactly the moments the standard should be stabilising the system.

explanation: A lifecycle standard gates each transition on phase-appropriate evidence: success criteria and an evaluation set before a pilot; measured results on real traffic, runbooks and ownership before handoff; and explicit monitoring thresholds that trigger iteration. Demos, confidence and feature counts are not gates.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide — Domain 6: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
